newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia ski lodge toll rises, hopes fading.
newsitem.headline: Australia ski lodge toll rises, hopes fading.

text.p: The official death toll in Australia's ski lodge landslide disaster rose to three on Friday and officials said there was little hope that any of the 17 people still missing under tonnes of rubble were alive after two nights of freezing temperatures.
One body was recovered overnight.

"Today we have located a further two (bodies)," fire brigade spokesman Ian Krimmer told Reuters. "We cannot determine their sex. They are still in situation. That brings it to a total of three," he said.
A landslide on Wednesday night destroyed two ski lodges and buried 20 people at Thredbo Alpine Village, Australia's most popular ski resort about 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney.

Rescuers on Friday continued the grim and dangerous task of digging by hand through rubble, rocks and mud in the small mountain village, but police say sub-zero temperatures means there is little chance anyone who survived the initial impact is still alive and hopes are fading by the hour.
"I think at this stage the chances are quite remote," Assistant Commissioner Ken Moroney told reporters, but he added that rescuers had not given up all hope.
Rescue officials said efforts would continue to concentrate on finding survivors and it was not known when the bodies found on Friday would be removed.

"We would hope to locate additional persons ... and one can always entertain a degree of hope they will be alive," Moroney said. "But ... the nature of time and the nature of the weather probably allows us to entertain some degree of concern."
Rescuers using fibre optic cameras and thermal imaging equipment have found no signs of life in the wreckage of the Carinya and Bimbadeen lodges.
Relatives of the missing rushed to Thredbo and were being briefed by police and offered the help of grief counsellors.
A total of 500 emergency workers are involved in the operation, sifting by hand through tonnes of soil, rock and trees, concrete and metal left in the wake of the landslide.
The search for survivors remained painstakingly slow in the freezing conditions, with the temperature falling to a low of minus 9 degrees Celsius (16 degrees Fahrenheit) overnight.
Rescuers were working under floodlights in shifts of two hours, followed by four hours of rest.
They were also being forced to shore up the site as they work to prevent further slides, a danger that delayed any concerted rescue effort for 10 hours after the initial landslide.
"The area still remains unstable," a police spokesman said.
Police said the those trapped in the slide included a middle-aged couple from California, a New Zealand woman and 17 Australians.
Messages of sympathy poured in from around the world to the small, close-knit community which has a population of up to 4,000 in the skiing season and a summer population of about 500.

Britian's Queen Elizabeth, who is also Australia's head of state, sent a message of sympathy to the victims' friends and families, Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer cut short an official visit to Japan, and Prime Minister John Howard issued a special statement of sympathy.
New South Wales state premier Bob Carr toured the site on Friday and talked with victims' relatives.
Church services have been held in Thredbo and in Canberra, attended by government dignitaries and community leaders.
Experts believe seepage from a mountain spring may have caused the earth to give way.
